title: AI CLINICAL SCRIBE — WEB & MOBILE PLATFORM
description: Web and mobile platform that listens to care visits and drafts the clinical note for review, backed by an agentic AI assistant that plans, calls tools across the clinic's data, and asks before it writes anything.

caseStudy.overview: A web and mobile platform for clinicians who visit patients and then have to write everything up by hand. It records the visit, transcribes who said what, drafts a structured clinical note, and hands it back to the clinician to review and approve. The same product also runs the day around the visit: patients, the appointment book, charting and an AI assistant. Behind it sits an agentic AI assistant that can look things up, build plans and take actions across the clinic's systems, with a person confirming anything that changes data. The mobile app (iOS and Android, built with Expo and React Native) puts the scribe, the appointment book and the patient list in the clinician's pocket, so a nurse in a patient's living room can record and review a visit without a laptop.
caseStudy.problem: In the US, nurses and other clinicians often travel to patients' homes or see back-to-back appointments, and every visit ends with documentation. Notes get typed up between visits, after hours, or from memory. That is slow, tiring, and the first thing to go wrong when a day runs long: details are missed, charts fall behind, and clinicians burn out on admin instead of care. Generic dictation tools did not help much, because the output was a wall of text, not a note in the shape the chart needs. The people who most need less paperwork are the ones away from a desk, so a web-only tool leaves the home-visit case unsolved.
caseStudy.approach: I treated the note as the product and the recording as the input. The visit is captured live, streamed for transcription with speaker turns, and turned into a structured note (summary, SOAP sections, action items and decisions) tied to the right patient and booking. The clinician is always the last step: they read the draft, fix it, and approve it before anything is exported or written back. Everything around it (today's visits, patient context, the appointment book) exists so the right patient is attached to a recording before it starts and the clinician rarely has to search for anything. For the road, I rebuilt the product's phone experience natively in React Native, using the web code as the specification: the same sections in the same order, the same wording, status rules and backend endpoints, with native touches (haptics, bottom sheets, share sheet, on-device speech) where the phone does it better. Each rebuilt area shipped with its own parity document, so reviewers know what matches and what deliberately differs.
features: Consent-first recording flow with live transcript and speaker turns
Structured notes: summary, SOAP sections, action items and decisions
Today's visits view that attaches a recording to the right booking
Review and approval step before copy, export or write-back to the record
Audio playback synced to the transcript, with markers and comments
Sharing with access by role, PDF and transcript export
Appointment book with day, week and per-provider load views
Patient profiles with visit history, charts, photos and linked scribes
Mobile app for iOS and Android with AI Scribe, Appointments and Patients tabs and a More menu
Native recording flow with consent dialog, speaker turns, floating dock and visit-context sheet
Role-aware tab gating, including a scribe-only mode
Guided tour, in-app user guide, support reporting and settings on mobile
Times shown in the clinic's own time zone, not the phone's
Agentic assistant with tool use, MCP, retrieval and confirm-before-write actions
AI assistant chat over WebSockets with a voice mode and file attachments
Inbox, approvals, charting and billing workspaces alongside the scribe and appointment book
EHR connections set up from Settings, with more integrations behind feature flags
Feature flags and role-based access so each workspace sees only what it should

challenges.title: Recording that survives real conditions
challenges.text: Microphones get blocked, tabs lose focus, and networks drop mid-visit. The recording flow handles permission errors with plain explanations, pauses and resumes cleanly, keeps the audio when note generation fails, and offers a retry instead of losing the visit.

challenges.title: Long-running AI work in a fast UI
challenges.text: A note is not ready the moment recording stops. The list and note pages poll for processing, failed and write-back states, show the reason for a failure by error code, and let the clinician keep working while the note is generated.

challenges.title: Trust in a clinical setting
challenges.text: Nothing is final until a person approves it. Approval gates the exports, status rules decide what a clinician can do next, and multi-tenant headers and role checks keep each clinic's data separate.

challenges.title: A big product, kept safe to change
challenges.text: The app grew to many modules with several people shipping at once. An atomic component system, strict design tokens, lint and type checks on every push, and four test lanes (unit, mocked end-to-end, live-API, pre-push gate) kept changes reviewable.

challenges.title: Parity without copy-paste
challenges.text: React on the web and React Native do not share components. I matched layout, copy and behaviour by reading the web source and rebuilding it with NativeWind, then recorded every intentional difference so parity stays a checkable claim, not a feeling.

challenges.title: Native speech and audio
challenges.text: Live speech recognition needs native modules, so it does not work in Expo Go. I built it on a development build, and made the app degrade safely: no crash when the native microphone module is missing, and clear errors when permission is denied or the mic stops.

challenges.title: Time zones and real-world data
challenges.text: Visits happen in the clinic's time zone, and some phones do not recognise every zone. I moved all schedule and recording times to the clinic's clock and added a guard so an unknown zone falls back instead of crashing.

challenges.title: Staying current on a fast-moving platform
challenges.text: I upgraded the app from Expo SDK 54 to 58 and React Native 0.88, replaced the removed audio library with the new one, and updated navigation, keeping the app building and shippable through EAS for both stores.

architecture: Next.js 15 App Router with React 18 and TypeScript; server route handlers for auth, layout, support and proxying
Redux Toolkit and RTK Query for data, with contract tests against shared fixtures and schemas
WebSocket layer for chat and live transcription, kept opt-in so the text flow is never affected
Cookie-based session checks in middleware protect every dashboard route
Tailwind design tokens with Shadcn UI and dark/light themes; Biome and Lefthook enforce quality
Expo SDK 58 and React Native 0.88 mobile app sharing Redux Toolkit / RTK Query API logic patterns with the web
NativeWind styling from the same design tokens as the web
expo-speech-recognition and expo-audio for capture and playback, expo-notifications for alerts
EAS Build profiles producing signed .aab and .ipa files for the stores
impact: Turns a free-form conversation into a structured note the clinician only has to review
Clinicians can start and finish documentation at the patient's side, on a phone
One mental model across web and phone, with documented parity per screen
An assistant that does the lookup and planning work, such as finding patients to call for open slots, instead of only answering questions
Moves documentation out of evenings and into the visit itself
One product covers the visit, the schedule and the patient record, so context follows the clinician
Predictable releases through layered automated testing and CI gates

agentic.intro: The assistant is not a chatbot bolted onto the product. It is an agent: it reads the question, decides which tools it needs, calls them, looks at what came back, and repeats until it can answer, all streamed to the clinician as it works.

steps.title: Classify, then plan
steps.text: Each message is classified first (a patient lookup, a schedule question, a search, a request to act) so the model starts with the right tools and instructions instead of every tool at once.

steps.title: A multi-turn tool loop
steps.text: The model runs a reason, act, observe loop of up to 15 turns. It asks for a tool, gets the result, and decides the next step, so a question like "who could fill Thursday's open slot" becomes several dependent lookups ending in one short answer.

steps.title: One registry for every kind of tool
steps.text: Built-in functions, Lambda-backed data views and MCP servers all sit behind a single tool registry with the same contract: a definition, an executor and metadata. Adding a capability means registering a tool, not changing the agent.

steps.title: Parallel when safe, sequential when not
steps.text: An execution strategy detects dependencies between requested tools (pagination, a read that needs an earlier write) and runs independent calls in parallel, with per-source limits, and dependent ones in order.

steps.title: Built to fail gracefully
steps.text: Each tool has retries with exponential backoff, a circuit breaker and a fallback chain, so if the structured query fails the agent drops back to search instead of giving up. Failed calls come back to the model as data it can reason about.

steps.title: Grounded retrieval and memory
steps.text: Search fans out to the knowledge base, the database and conversation memory in parallel, then fuses, de-duplicates and reranks. Conversation summaries and patient context are stored per clinic, so answers stay consistent across sessions.

steps.title: Safe by construction
steps.text: Every tool call carries the clinic, user and patient context, and access is checked per request. Writes and sends need the user's confirmation. Content from uploaded files is treated as data, never instructions, which also guards against prompt injection.

steps.title: Rich results, not just text
steps.text: Tools return structured attachments (patient photos, documents, chart links, a live fill plan for open appointment slots) that the apps render as cards. The model only sees references, so no links or private data are made up or leaked.

steps.title: Observable and tested
steps.text: OpenTelemetry-style traces, metrics and token budgets cover every turn, and eval suites for routing and conversations catch regressions when prompts, tools or models change.

llm.heading: From conversation to clinical note
llm.intro: The hard part was not getting a model to write a note. It was getting a note a busy clinician would actually read, trust and approve. The design choice that mattered most: capture the visit once as structured facts, and draw everything a person reads from those facts.

steps.title: Transcribe with speaker turns
steps.text: Audio is transcribed as the visit happens, with turns attributed to speakers, so the model works from who said what and not from one block of text.

steps.title: Extract typed visit facts, once
steps.text: A single model call turns the transcript into typed groups of short, one-line facts. It replaced a separate SOAP-writing call, so there is one extraction and one source of truth instead of several prompts that can disagree.

steps.title: Every note is a view of the facts
steps.text: The SOAP note, the summary and the chart are all rendered from the same facts. This came from a real complaint that notes were far too long. The fix was structural, not another prompt tweak: change the view, not the extraction.

steps.title: Write the way each provider writes
steps.text: Charting profiles learn how each provider writes from charts they have already filled in: a few words per field, or lists. Drafts follow that style and the clinic's own chart templates, so nobody re-types the note into the form they know.

steps.title: Note views and learned style
steps.text: Each reader can choose brief, detailed or paragraph summaries, resolved from provider to role to clinic to learned style. When someone shortens or deletes sections, the system suggests a view, but never applies it on its own.

steps.title: Intent routing that never blocks
steps.text: A semantic router reads each assistant message in parallel and picks the intent and likely tools. It is trained on labelled examples across many intents, calibrated, and tested on a held-out set written by someone who never saw the training data. It guides the turn but never gates it.

steps.title: Reliable under real load
steps.text: Claude is the primary model, with a second provider as fallback when the first is over quota, overloaded or silent, applied only when nothing has reached the user's screen. Prompt caching, per-turn token budgets, a rate-limit ledger and conversation checkpoints with summaries keep long sessions fast and within limits.

steps.title: Grounded, safe and measured
steps.text: Responses are checked for hallucination and confidence, tenant isolation is tested with red-team cases, uploaded content is treated as data and not instructions, and a person approves every note. Evals run the real prompt and tools end to end with strict structural checks, and are re-run whenever the model, prompt or tools change.

title: ENTERPRISE MULTI-AGENT AI ASSISTANT
description: Employee-facing financial assistant built on a supervisor with specialist sub-agents for accounts, loans, contributions, beneficiaries and enrollment, with RAG grounding, integrated guardrails, evals and prompt tracing across dev, staging and production.

caseStudy.overview: A chat assistant for a company's employees that answers questions and gets financial and benefits tasks done in one place. Behind a single chat window, a supervisor agent routes each request to a specialist sub-agent (self-directed account, loan, contribution, beneficiary, enrollment and more), grounded in the company's own documents and data. Every message passes through guardrails on the way in and on the way out, and every prompt is traced and evaluated across environments.
caseStudy.problem: Employees had to hunt through portals, PDFs and phone queues to answer questions about loans, contributions, beneficiaries or enrolling in a plan, and each topic lived in a different system. A single general-purpose chatbot was not an option: financial answers must be correct, grounded in the right policy, and safe, and a wrong or leaky answer has real consequences. The company also had an internal team that owned AI safety policy, so the assistant had to plug into their guardrails and not invent its own.
caseStudy.approach: As the lead on this project, I made the architecture decisions, worked directly with the client and reviewed the team's work. I split the problem the way the business is split. A supervisor agent classifies intent and delegates to domain sub-agents, each with its own tools, knowledge and instructions, orchestrated with LangGraph and run on AWS Bedrock AgentCore. Retrieval keeps answers grounded in company content. Around the agents I integrated the internal team's guardrails web app on both input and output, then went beyond wiring it up: I built the evaluation sets, drove down false positives, and set up monitoring and tracing for prompts in dev, staging and production, so quality and safety could be measured and not assumed.

agentic.intro: The assistant is a team of agents, not one prompt. A supervisor understands the request and hands it to the specialist that owns that part of the business, then assembles one clear answer for the employee.

steps.title: Supervisor agent
steps.text: Classifies each message, keeps the conversation state, decides which specialist (or several) should act, and merges their results into a single reply. Ambiguous requests get a clarifying question instead of a guess.

steps.title: Specialist sub-agents
steps.text: Separate agents for self-directed accounts, loans, contributions, beneficiaries and enrollment, each with its own tools, data access and instructions, so each stays small, testable and easy to change without touching the others.

steps.title: LangGraph orchestration
steps.text: The flow is a LangGraph graph: nodes for routing, tool calls, retrieval and response, with explicit state and edges. That makes handoffs, retries and human-in-the-loop steps predictable and easy to trace.

steps.title: Bedrock AgentCore runtime
steps.text: Agents run on AWS Bedrock AgentCore, which handles hosting, identity and memory for the agents, so the team focused on behaviour rather than infrastructure.

steps.title: Grounded with RAG
steps.text: Policy documents and plan rules are ingested, chunked and embedded. Sub-agents retrieve the relevant passages and answer from them, with sources, to cut hallucinations on rules that must be exact.

steps.title: Tools with real actions
steps.text: Agents call internal APIs to read balances, start a request or update a record. Anything that changes data is explicit and confirmed with the employee first.

steps.title: Guardrails on the way in and out
steps.text: Each user message is checked before an agent sees it, and each answer is checked before the user sees it, using the internal team's guardrails service. Blocked content gets a safe, helpful fallback.

steps.title: Evals, tracing and monitoring
steps.text: Every prompt and response is traced across dev, staging and production. Evals score routing, retrieval, answers and guardrail decisions, and the scores are watched on dashboards, so a change to a prompt, model or tool shows up as a number before it reaches employees.

features: One chat for loans, contributions, beneficiaries, enrollment and self-directed accounts
Supervisor and specialist sub-agents, each with its own tools and knowledge
Retrieval grounded in company policy documents, with sources
Integrated internal guardrails on both input and output
Evals and scoring across routing, retrieval, answers and guardrails, using logic-based checks and LLM-as-judge
False-positive reduction so safe questions are not blocked
End-to-end tracing and monitoring of prompts in dev, staging and production
Confirm-before-act for anything that changes an employee's data

challenges.title: Guardrails that protect without blocking
challenges.text: Early on, legitimate questions about loans or beneficiaries were being flagged. I collected those cases into a labelled set, found the patterns behind each false positive, and worked with the guardrails owners and the prompts to fix them, re-running the full set after every change so fixes never reopened real risks.

challenges.title: Two kinds of checks, used where each fits
challenges.text: Some input and output checks are deterministic logic: pattern and rule checks that are fast, cheap and explainable, for things like sensitive identifiers. Others need judgement, so an LLM acts as judge with a written rubric for relevance, groundedness and policy. Choosing the right kind for each check kept cost and latency down without losing coverage.

challenges.title: Measuring quality, not guessing
challenges.text: The evals cover the whole pipeline, not just the final answer: routing (did the supervisor pick the right sub-agent), tool selection, retrieval, answer correctness and guardrail decisions on input and output. Each run is scored, with logic-based scores where an answer can be checked exactly and an LLM judge with a rubric where it needs judgement, and the scores are tracked per prompt version and per environment. A prompt or model change has to hold those scores before it moves from dev to staging to production.

challenges.title: Seeing inside a multi-agent run
challenges.text: A single question can touch a supervisor, two sub-agents, retrieval and several tools. Tracing every step with the same prompt versions in each environment made it possible to find which agent or prompt caused a bad answer, and to compare dev, staging and production behaviour.

challenges.title: Working across teams
challenges.text: The guardrails belong to another team. I integrated against their service and contract, fed back the false positives and gaps I found, and agreed how policy changes roll out, so the safety team and the product team could move without blocking each other.

challenges.title: Leading the work
challenges.text: I was the main contact for the client, translating their needs into a plan, deciding the agent design and evaluation approach, dividing the work across the team and reviewing it, so the pieces fit together and shipped with confidence.

architecture: Next.js chat UI streaming responses from the backend
Supervisor and sub-agents orchestrated as a LangGraph graph, hosted on AWS Bedrock AgentCore
Retrieval layer over a vector store for policy and plan documents
Guardrails service called before the agents (input) and before the reply (output)
Tracing and monitoring per prompt and per environment, with eval jobs scoring samples
Separate dev, staging and production configurations with promoted prompt versions
impact: One place for employees to ask about and act on their financial benefits
Answers grounded in company documents, with fewer hallucinations
Safety policy enforced consistently on every input and output
Fewer false-positive blocks, so the assistant stays useful
Prompt and model changes are measured before release, not after

title: ENGINEERING KNOWLEDGE MCP PIPELINE
description: A merge-triggered pipeline that keeps every repo's code and design knowledge embedded in S3 Vectors, served to employees and agents through FastMCP servers and Bedrock AgentCore.

caseStudy.overview: An internal platform that turns a company's many repositories into one searchable, always-current knowledge layer. Each time a project is merged into its main branch, a pipeline re-embeds what changed and updates the vector store. MCP servers then expose that knowledge to employees and AI agents, so anyone can ask how a system is designed, how a service works or where something lives, without hunting through repos.
caseStudy.problem: The company had many projects and repositories across different technologies, each with its own system design, conventions and decisions. Knowledge lived in code and scattered docs, went stale as soon as it was written down, and was only really known by the people who built it. New joiners and other teams lost days finding answers, and AI assistants could not help because they had no access to the company's own systems. A one-time import would not fix it, since the code changes every day.
caseStudy.approach: I made freshness the core of the design: knowledge updates when code does. A pipeline listens for merges to main or master across all repositories, processes only what changed, and keeps the index in sync. The knowledge is organised into collections, one per project, so results stay relevant and access can be controlled. Retrieval is exposed through MCP servers built with FastMCP, the standard way for AI tools and agents to use external knowledge, and the same servers feed an agent running on Bedrock AgentCore. Claude, through the Anthropic API, is used to understand code and documents so that what gets embedded is meaningful and not raw text.

agentic.intro: The system has two halves: a pipeline that keeps knowledge current, and MCP servers that let people and agents use it.

steps.title: Merge triggers the pipeline
steps.text: A merge into main or master in any connected repository starts the run. Many repositories, written in different languages and frameworks, all feed the same flow without each team changing how they work.

steps.title: Process only what changed
steps.text: The pipeline reads the diff, not the whole repository, and picks out the files, docs and design notes that changed. That keeps runs fast and cheap, and means the index reflects the main branch within minutes.

steps.title: Understand before embedding
steps.text: Code and documents are split into meaningful units that suit their language and type. Claude, via the Anthropic API, adds summaries and context, so a function, a service or a design decision is embedded together with what it does and why.

steps.title: Embeddings in S3 Vectors
steps.text: Embeddings are stored in S3 Vectors, so the index is durable, scales with the number of repositories and avoids running a separate vector database. Changed items are upserted and deleted code is removed, so nothing stale is returned.

steps.title: Collections per project
steps.text: Each project has its own collection. Searches can target one system or span many, and access can follow who is allowed to see which project.

steps.title: FastMCP servers
steps.text: MCP servers built with FastMCP expose tools for searching a collection, listing projects and reading a result in context. Once connected, an employee's AI tool can use the company's knowledge directly from the editor or chat.

steps.title: Agents on AgentCore
steps.text: An agent on AWS Bedrock AgentCore uses the same MCP tools, so it can answer cross-project questions, compare designs and point to the source, with the retrieved content as grounding.

steps.title: Observable and safe to run
steps.text: Each pipeline run is logged with what was processed, added and removed, and failures are visible and retryable, so a broken repository does not quietly leave the index out of date.

features: Merge-triggered pipeline across many repositories and technologies
Incremental updates that process only what changed
Embeddings stored in S3 Vectors, organised in collections per project
FastMCP servers that expose search and lookup tools
Claude via the Anthropic API to summarise and add context before embedding
Agents on Bedrock AgentCore using the same MCP tools
Removal of deleted code so results never go stale
Run logs and retries for every pipeline execution

challenges.title: Many repos, many technologies
challenges.text: Different languages and project layouts need different parsing and chunking. A common pipeline with per-type handling let a new repository join without custom work.

challenges.title: Staying fresh without re-indexing everything
challenges.text: Re-embedding every repository on every merge would be slow and costly. Working from the diff, and deleting what was removed, kept the index current at a fraction of the cost.

challenges.title: Useful chunks, not just text
challenges.text: Raw code embeds poorly. Adding a clear summary and context to each unit with Claude made retrieval return the right function, service or decision, not a near-match.

challenges.title: One interface for people and agents
challenges.text: By serving everything through MCP, the same knowledge works in an employee's AI tool and in an AgentCore agent, with no separate integration for each.

architecture: Repository merge events to main or master start a CI pipeline per project
Diff-based processing, then Claude via the Anthropic API for summaries and context
Embeddings upserted to S3 Vectors, with one collection per project
FastMCP servers expose search and read tools over the collections
AWS Bedrock AgentCore agents and employee AI tools connect as MCP clients
impact: Engineering knowledge that updates itself as code is merged
Faster onboarding and fewer interruptions for the people who built each system
Employees and agents can query every project's design from one place
A reusable pattern: connect a repository once and its knowledge stays current

title: EVENT DISCOVERY & TICKET BOOKING PLATFORM
description: End-to-end event discovery and ticket booking product across mobile and web: Expo apps, REST APIs documented in Swagger, SNS and SQS for async work and notifications, and Grafana monitoring.

caseStudy.overview: A consumer platform focused only on events and experiences, in the spirit of the big entertainment-booking apps but without the movies and everything else: browse what's on nearby, join communities around what you like, invite friends, book tickets, and get confirmations and reminders. I led the team and owned the product end to end: the mobile app, the web app, the backend and the cloud setup behind them, from the first screen and API design to logging and monitoring in production, while staying hands-on in the code.
caseStudy.problem: The big booking apps try to do everything: movies, sports, plays and events all in one feed. Live events and experiences, such as concerts, festivals, workshops and nightlife, get buried between blockbuster listings, and the app is built around movie-style booking, not around discovering something worth going to. People who want an experience have to dig for it, there is no sense of community around the things they love, and organisers of smaller events struggle to be seen and to build a following. And a booking product has its own hard parts: traffic spikes around popular events, notifications that are missed or sent twice, and failures that are hard to notice and debug without good logging and monitoring.
caseStudy.approach: I designed it as one product focused only on events and experiences, with shared foundations, and led its build across every layer: I made the architecture and technology decisions, worked directly with the client to shape scope and priorities, divided the work across the team and reviewed their code. Expo powers the mobile app and the web app from the same React and TypeScript knowledge and shared logic. A REST backend, documented with Swagger so the front ends and the team always work from one contract, handles events, bookings and users. Anything that doesn't have to happen while the user waits, such as confirmations, reminders and notification fan-out, goes through SNS and SQS so it is reliable and absorbs traffic spikes. Logging and monitoring were part of the build from day one, with Grafana dashboards over logs and metrics.
features: Event discovery focused on experiences, with search, categories and nearby results
Communities around interests and organisers, where people meet before and after events
Follow organisers and communities to hear about new events first
Share events and invite friends, so going together is easy
Event details, ticket selection and a smooth booking flow
User profiles, saved events and a booking history
Push, email and in-app notifications for confirmations, reminders and community updates
Mobile app on iOS and Android and a web app from the same Expo codebase
REST APIs with Swagger documentation for every endpoint
Asynchronous processing with SNS topics and SQS queues
Centralised logging with Grafana dashboards and alerts

challenges.title: One product on mobile and web
challenges.text: Using Expo for both mobile and web kept screens, navigation and business logic consistent, while platform-specific details (gestures, permissions, push tokens, responsive layouts) were handled where they differ.

challenges.title: Reliable notifications
challenges.text: A booking should produce exactly one confirmation, even if a service retries. Publishing events to SNS and consuming them from SQS, with idempotent handlers and dead-letter queues, made notifications dependable and kept slow or failing channels from affecting bookings.

challenges.title: Handling booking spikes
challenges.text: Popular events create bursts of traffic. Queues smooth the load on downstream work, and the API stays responsive because the user-facing path only does what the user has to wait for.

challenges.title: One source of truth for the API
challenges.text: Swagger-documented REST endpoints gave the web and mobile clients and the backend one contract, with examples and schemas to test against instead of guesses, which kept every developer on the team building against the same agreed contract.

challenges.title: Knowing when something breaks
challenges.text: Structured logs and metrics feed Grafana dashboards and alerts, so failed payments, stuck queues or slow endpoints show up as a graph and a notification, not as a user complaint.

challenges.title: Leading the team and the client
challenges.text: Beyond the code, I ran the conversations with the client, turned their goals into scoped work, made the calls on trade-offs, split tasks across the team and reviewed pull requests, so quality and delivery stayed predictable.

architecture: Expo (React Native and web) with TypeScript for the mobile and web clients
REST API backend with Swagger / OpenAPI documentation
SNS topics and SQS queues for confirmations, reminders and notification delivery, with retries and dead-letter queues
Push, email and in-app notification channels behind a single notification service
Structured logging and metrics visualised in Grafana, with alerting
impact: Events become a social experience, with communities and sharing that bring people back
A product taken from idea to production on iOS, Android and the web under one technical lead, with clear ownership and reviewed code
Reliable, deduplicated notifications even under retries and traffic spikes
A documented API contract that keeps the clients and backend in sync
Production issues visible on dashboards and alerts before users report them

title: EMBEDDABLE AUTH COMPONENT BUILDER
description: A SaaS where teams design their own sign-up and login experience, customising buttons, colours, fields and layout, then drop it into any project as an embed link or component.

caseStudy.overview: A SaaS product that lets teams build and brand their own authentication screens without writing UI code. Users configure sign-up, login and related flows in a builder: which fields appear, how the auth buttons look, colours, layout and more. When they are done, they get an embed link or a ready-to-use component to paste into their own project, on any framework.
caseStudy.problem: Every product needs sign-up and login, and every team ends up rebuilding the same screens: forms, validation, social buttons, error states, branding. Off-the-shelf widgets are rigid or tie you to a framework, so they either clash with your design or can't be used outside React. Teams wanted the speed of a ready-made flow, full control of how it looks, and a way to ship it into any stack.
caseStudy.approach: I built the auth UI as framework-agnostic web components with Stencil.js, so one implementation works in plain HTML, React, Vue, Angular or anything else. A React wrapper gives React teams a native-feeling component, and a monorepo keeps the web components, the React wrapper, the builder app and shared configuration in one place so they version and ship together. The key design choice was a configuration schema: every option in the builder is data (fields, buttons, theme tokens, layout), and the components render purely from that configuration. The builder edits the config with a live preview, and the same config produces the embed link or component the customer installs.
features: Sign-up, login and related auth flows as ready-made components
Builder to customise fields, auth buttons, colours, typography and layout
Live preview that updates as the configuration changes
Framework-agnostic web components built with Stencil.js
React wrapper for a native-feeling component in React apps
Embed link or component output to drop into any project
Configuration-driven rendering, so a design is just saved data
Monorepo with shared packages for the components, wrapper and builder

challenges.title: One component, any framework
challenges.text: Web components work everywhere, but frameworks handle props, events and styling differently. Stencil produced the standards-based components, and a thin React wrapper smoothed over the differences so React teams get typed props and normal event handling.

challenges.title: Customisable without becoming chaos
challenges.text: Giving users control over fields, colours and layout can easily produce broken or inaccessible screens. A typed configuration schema with defaults and validation kept every combination renderable, and design tokens kept theming consistent.

challenges.title: Styling inside someone else's app
challenges.text: Embedded components must not break, or be broken by, the host page's CSS. Encapsulated styles with exposed theme variables let each customer match the component to their brand safely.

challenges.title: Keeping several packages in step
challenges.text: The components, the React wrapper and the builder all depend on the same configuration schema. A monorepo with shared packages meant a schema change updated them together, and the preview in the builder always matched what customers would ship.

architecture: Monorepo containing the web components, the React wrapper, the builder app and shared config packages
Stencil.js web components that render entirely from a configuration object
React wrapper package that exposes the components with typed props and events
Builder app that edits and validates the configuration with a live preview
Output as an embed link or an installable component using the saved configuration
impact: Teams get a branded, working auth flow without building the UI
The same component works in any framework, so customers are not locked in
A configuration-first design that makes new options and themes cheap to add
One monorepo that keeps components, wrapper and builder consistent
